utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. [French on the English channel] On channel four, we have the French translation at the moment. Hopefully we can -- I think now this problem is solved. Again, good morning and, especially to you, Ms. Hasan, it's the first time that I see you in the courtroom this year and we wish you a successful year. As you see, Judge Mindua is not with us this morning. He has an urgent medical appointment. The Chamber decided to sit only with two judges, pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Your Honour, the Defence wants to respond orally to the Prosecution's motion of the 2nd of February 2011, if that is all right with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution's motion dated 2 February 2011 is moot in the view of the Defence, because it has already been contained in the supplemental information provided by the Prosecution in accordance to Rule 74 bis on the 26th of November 2010. That's why this motion should be rejected. As far as two reports by Mr. Brunborg, we are still awaiting decision on the Prosecution's motion that has been contained in the motion according to 94 bis in November 2009 as well as our response that was filed on the 11th of January 2010. As far as the report of Mr. Brunborg itself and the supplemental information to that report, all that has been translated into Serbian and it has also been given to the Defence back in January 2010. Let me also remind you that the Defence in its motion of the 11th of January 2010 already stated that it would not accept his report and that he -- that the Defence wants to cross-examine the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your position is surprising. Of course, the witness will be cross-examined this week. He will appear in the courtroom tomorrow. Ms. Hasan, do you want to respond to Mr. Gajic? Or Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Brunborg is my witness so he will be ready to start on Tuesday and it looks like we are going to take up most of Monday with other witnesses, and his reports of 2009 have been part of our motion for a long time. The Defence has been on notice of those reports and we merely want to get them a 65 ter number so that I can ask him briefly about them when he testifies. So we are satisfied with our motion and that we now see what the Defence has said but I don't think anything else need be said unless you have some questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the application and the statement of the Defence, and we will come back to that matter in the course of today. I have to raise two other problems. There was a problem with some documents marked for identification related to Witness Dr. Haglund, and there was some discussion between the parties about translation of some of these documents. Did the parties reach an agreement on that? Which of these documents should be translated? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We haven't reached anything formal yet, but we did show the Defence some of the material that hadn't been translated and it was largely massive charts and numbers which Mr. Gajic agreed did not need to be translated so we'll get together again and see if there is anything that he does feel needs to be translated to see what we could either agree on or agree to disagree on but we are getting closer. Just other things took over but we'll get back together and I'm sure as we always do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are awaiting your common position. The third point, documents tendered and received by the Chamber pursuant to the 92 bis decision. In the meantime we received a list of 19 of these documents which have no translation yet. We have to reverse these documents from admitted documents to marked for identification pending translation. These 19 exhibits, I think it is the best way to read it out into the record by the registrar, so that we have it clear on the record that they are only marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the following documents shall be marked for identification, reclassified from exhibit status. P1538E, P1538F, P1538G, P1541C, P1542C, P1542D, P1543C, P1544C, P1562C, P1563C, P1565B, P1569B, P1569C, P1571B, P1660, P1661, P1677, P1678, and P1690. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are there other matters to raise at this point in time? I don't think so. The witness should be brought in, please. We are turning into closed session to enable the witness to enter the courtroom because of protective measures of face distortion.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, good morning, sir, as you can see there are only two judges on the Bench today, but different from last Thursday, but this is according to our rules. The affirmation to tell the truth you made last Thursday still applies. And Ms. Hasan is continuing the cross-examination -- the examination-in-chief. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simanic. In July 1995 were there any other sources other than the 5th Engineering Battalion stationed in the Konjevic Polje area?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Konjevic Polje, in July 1995, there was a police check-point manned by the police forces. They worked in shifts and I had absolutely no insight in their work because they worked according to their plans and their orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And which police are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the school. They had the permanent check-point at the intersection in Konjevic Polje. Its purpose was to monitor the road, I suppose most probably because that's where they were most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall the uniform they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see, the uniforms were blue, camouflage blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: All right. The 5th Engineering Battalion, was it subdivided into companies?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th Engineering Battalion existed only in paper as a battalion because the manpower was maybe as high as a company. However, it was divided into companies but those companies were very small. So they only held a formal title of company, however, the units themselves were smaller and contained a smaller number of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell me the names of those companies?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, there was the Pioneer Company, then there was the company for roads and bridges, then there was the construction company or engineering company, I'm not quite sure what the name was. And then there was the Pontoon Company.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In the days following the fall of Srebrenica, the 11th, 12th and 13th of July 1995, was the 5th Engineering Battalion under any threat?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what kind of threat you have in mind. However, we learned from the soldiers who would come from their rest periods what was going on in the surroundings. We also had another big problem. Two of our guards, two of our soldiers, were wounded at the guard post number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What did you learn about what was going on in your surroundings?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We learned what is contained in a report. A group of the B and H army from Srebrenica is moving through the region. Some of them are already hors de combat, others not yet. So we did not know exactly what the situation was. We tried to solve our situation as best as we could by providing security for our own barracks bearing in mind the number of men that we had at our disposal which was quite low at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And when you say you were providing security, was that defending against this group of people that were coming through?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that through the barracks itself any of the groups passed, but we heard some things and we had a duty to provide security to the barracks. It was also our permanent duty, even if the situation was not as it was, because the barracks contained the warehouse of ammunition and ordnance.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what exactly did you do to secure the barracks and the depot containing the materials?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we reinforced our guard posts. We also reinforced the security between the guard posts, and we secured a minefield, because with the number of men we had, we couldn't provide a high-quality security to the zone of the barracks. That's why, instead, we used minefields on the left and right side of the road when you look from Konjevic Polje in the direction of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And did any of the companies of your battalion have combat tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of combat tasks do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, any combat tasks, engaging the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, if you consider laying out a minefield a combat task, then I can tell you that that was the basic task of the Pioneer Company. On the other hand, if you are referring to ambushes that I mentioned in my previous statements, that was something that was done solely as part of the security of the barracks and the minefield. So whenever we had enough manpower, we would usually during the night establish ambushes, that's how we were told to call them, and I suppose that's what is contained in the reports and that was only between the exits and the minefields. During the day on the other hand, because the visibility was better, we only had guard posts and we had a minimal number of men manning the guard posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall the members of your battalion that were wounded at this time?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right then, while this was going on, I was not in Konjevic Polje but I knew those people because they were members of the battalion. They were older people. In fact, most of the members of the battalion were older people. We couldn't send them into action or to any sort of work because they were either unable to work or they could work only little.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: How did you learn that these soldiers were injured?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned to Konjevic Polje, then I learned that they were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall when you returned to Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the same day, in the evening. I think so. I can't remember it exactly right now because it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 2082 displayed on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: This is a report dated 14th July 1995, and it has a reference number of 107-2. Sir, could you just review this document, because I'm going to ask you a few questions about it in a moment. If I can just request the assistance of the court usher to hand the original to the witness to take a look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this is a document that contains information about the wounded, and it was addressed to the superior command, and here you can see it's the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Whose name does the document bear?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the 5th Engineering Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the signature on the first page of that document?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I signed it or not, but it does look like my signature, because you have to bear in mind that my signature usually varies. You can see the same thing if you look at the two different documents. You will see that I usually don't sign it the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And can you -- can we just turn to the second page of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do that, I would like to ask the witness if he can see the typed name above the signature, what is written there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mile Simanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the time, have you been the deputy commander of this battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I was. I was the deputy commander of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So on this second page, there is a stamp on the bottom of it. Does that also -- whose name is written there and can you tell us the title and -- and whether that's your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy commander, Major Mile Simanic, the same applies that I said earlier, the signatures are different. It's probably my signature but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What information were you forwarding to the Drina Corps command through this report?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see here, this is data about wounded persons in the 5th Engineering Battalion on the 13th of July, I think. It's an extraordinary report or event.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you report to the Drina Corps command about these wounded soldiers? Was this pursuant to an order?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see here, there was an order, I'm not familiar with the order, this was done by the administrative person who was in charge of all of that in our unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Was it your practice to report to the Drina Corps command any time soldiers were wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was. Well, it just turned out that I was there. Had the commander been there, he would have done it because we didn't have any wounded persons, any wounded soldiers, before.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And it states here that the soldiers were wounded while executing a combat task. Can you tell me, then, since you were there, what combat tasks these soldiers were engaged in?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I wasn't there when it actually happened. Their combat task was to secure the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to turn to another document, that's 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, are you tendering this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, I can do so at this. I would like to offer it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned exhibit number P1767, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could now turn to 65 ter 0012? Sorry, that's 00112.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: This appears to be an interim report. It's dated 13 July 1995, one day before the previous report we just looked at. Who were you -- if you could just review this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, is it possible to use the other microphone, to minimise the noise of the typing on that desk? Yes, it's much better now, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And who were you reporting to through this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that the interim report is being submitted to the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature at the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, it's similar to my signature. As for whether I signed it or not, well, the important thing is that what happened was so. It happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell me what is written on top of your signature, right by the stamp?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above my signature, it says, "Mile Simanic."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell me the purpose, then, of this interim report?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To inform the Drina Corps command and for them to do something to draw attention, because there were very few of us, to draw attention to the fact that we were being threatened, under threat, in that area. I must repeat here, it says correctly, during a combat assignment, at guard post number 6, that is the most forward guard post, and it's the closest to the beginning of a minefield.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell from this document when these soldiers were wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that they were wounded on the 13th of July, at approximately 0800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you testified that you arrived in Konjevic Polje after these soldiers were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the soldiers were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in light of this report, this interim report, and the previous report we looked at, which was dated 14th July 1995, would you have arrived in Konjevic Polje in the evening of the 13th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it's possible, but I don't really remember exactly when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In the first line of this, this report reads, "On 13th July 1995 an unusual incident occurred during which the following were wounded in carrying out their combat tasks in the struggle against enemy extremists and civilians infiltrated in the region of Pobudje Brdo" - excuse me for the pronunciation - "Konjevic Polje at around 0800 hours at guard post number 6." Are these the people -- are the enemy extremists and civilians referred to here the people you were mentioning that were passing through the region?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Probably they were meant by that, they were passing through. As far as I was informed and as far as I heard, they escaped so you couldn't really establish it quite specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we have this report tendered as the next exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put an additional question to the witness? If I'm not mistaken, you are referring to the same event in this document as in the previous document we have seen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. It's the same -- it's the same event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you tell me the reason why this event was reported to the Drina Corps command the same day twice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a reserve officer, so I don't understand military terminology or military administration all that well, so the administrator who was in charge, he was doing all these things. He says, "This is how it should be done" and this is how he did it, and I signed it. That's how it went, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, this document will be received as an exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit number P1768, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we just have the court usher retrieve the original document from the witness, and perhaps, if Your Honours, if you would like to take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, that is the first report we looked at. It's report dated the 14th of July 1995, which refers to the injured soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, the Pioneer Company, where were they located on the 11th, 12th and 13th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never used the company in its full composition at one place, so there were several places. I don't remember exactly how many places there were. One of them was at an elevation, Vis, it's a construction site in the area of the Kalesija municipality, the place is called Osmaci. There was a group also that was doing de-mining in one location. I'm trying to remember the name of the place. I can't remember the name right now. It's in the direction of Srebrenica, as you're going to Skelani, this was also a minefield that needed to be de-mined so I think they kind of came back in that period sometime. Some soldiers are always resting. A number of them were supposed to be at the passive reflector. This is a facility where some rocks needed to be mined. I can't remember exactly where that was. There was also a number of soldiers who went to de-mine a place behind Milici towards Srebrenica, behind Derventa. There was a road that was mined so they went to clear those mines there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What about the road and bridge company? Where were they located on the 11th, 12th and 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of our companies was alone in any construction site. We combined them because we did it according to the needs at the time. We combined the personnel. A number of them were at Vis, in the Kalesija municipality, as Osmaci, one of them at the reflector location above Vlasenica. A number were supposed to be carrying out preparations to build an electricity power line from Vlasenica to Konjevic Polje, to the approach roads there. Also, there was a number who was supposed to be in the Bisina barracks above Sekovici. I cannot give you the exact days and the number of men but this is something that you learn only after the tasks are completed. You draw up a report and then this is something that is then mentioned in the report, who carried out certain assignments, what was expended of the material in the execution of the task and how much time was needed to complete the task.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The engineering company of your battalion, where were they located and what were they doing during this same time period?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The engineering company, actually we called it the Construction Company, comprised skilled men. They were carpenters, construction workers, builders, and they mostly worked in places where there was some work on buildings, let's say, high-rise buildings or other buildings, needed by other units and higher-ranking units. A number were at the Bisina barracks. There was a barracks building that was being built there. A number were deployed among the other units at other construction sites, as needed. And then also a number of them were resting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Where was the Logistics Company at this time?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no logistics company. It was actually a platoon that had five or six women and a number of men, and they were billeted at Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you have a duty to report back to the Drina Corps command when any of the tasks that they ordered were completed?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each assignment proceeded pursuant to an order. We couldn't do any assignments unless there was an order to do them. After each such assignment we would submit a report with the exact number of people engaged on it, what was spent of material and equipment, how much time was required, and this report is then submitted to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall following that procedure in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why it wouldn't have been followed. I don't know exactly what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, we've looked at some of the reports that bear your signature, that went up to the Drina Corps command. We've seen the interim report. We've seen some of the other reports that were submitted pursuant to orders. Was there any other duty for your battalion to report to the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered that, that we were duty-bound to submit reports and we submitted the reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: How -- how often were these reports submitted to the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean upon completion of the task?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry, no, I was asking whether there were -- was any other duty for your battalion to report to the Drina Corps command about the activities of the various companies.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean combat reports?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were obliged to do that, and we sent them all the time. The administrative person was the one who took care of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what form of communication was used to submit these combat reports?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was delivered by hand. It would always say, "By courier" but there were no couriers in the sense that somebody especially came for that. It was more likely that somebody would be going to Vlasenica anyway and as they were going they would take the report and submit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And how often did you submit these reports to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: When were you required to submit the reports by, what time of day?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not really able to say until by what time of day. These reports were not all that important to me. Nobody harried us, nor was it important at what time of the day it arrived. Sometimes we would even be a whole day late. It depended on what time or when somebody would leave for Vlasenica, and that's when the report would be sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Who signed these reports?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would sign them, the commander would, when he was there, but if neither of us was there, somebody else would sign it, probably the duty officer would do that when it had to be sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Where was the commander Avramovic on the 11th, 12th and 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, he was on leave. I think his wife and daughter had come. I don't know exactly where he was. Somewhere in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Given his absence during that time period, whose responsibility was it to sign off on these reports?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned this earlier. If I was there, I would sign it. Sometimes I knew that I wouldn't be there at a certain time so I would just sign a blank report. We didn't really attach -- well, we were not that important actually. In a way, we were kind of tenants there. I mean maybe this is not appropriate military terminology but we didn't have an area of responsibility like the infantry units did. The place where we were was in the area of responsibility of another brigade. I think this was on the triangle between Bratunac, Srebrenica and Milici. So I'm not really sure exactly whose area of responsibility it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we now have 65 ter 1910 displayed on the screen, please? And if I could just request again the assistance of the Court usher to hand the original to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, if you could just take a moment to review and let me know when you're done.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, this report -- there is an indication on the first page of this report that this is a regular combat report. Would that have been one of the daily reports written to the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. It's a regular daily report, so that's what it should have, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What is the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 14th of July 1995 is what it states.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if you could just turn the page, turn your original, to the second page, and on e-court in English version it's the third page, B/C/S version the second page, could we just have the English then to the third page? Sorry, my mistake. I apologise. It's page 4 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us whose name is written right near that stamp on the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is Mile Simanic, that's my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it does look like mine, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Does that -- the text on top of your name there also state your title?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says Major and Deputy Commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Would you please now read aloud the text written under the first paragraph of this document so if we could revert back to page 1 of the B/C/S -- okay, I'll -- perhaps it's easier if I just read it and that is, the first page of the English and the first page of the B/C/S. It reads: "1, the enemy: A large enemy group was infiltrated into the region of Pobudje Brdo and the region of Konjevic Polje. Units of the 5th Engineering Battalion and the MUP, Ministry of Interior, successfully resisted the enemy. About 1.000 to 1.500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested and killed." Sir, do you remember what you said when you were first shown this document by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When do you mean? Here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, this could have been during an interview that you had with the Office of the Prosecutor in 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just to correct the transcript, it seems to me that Ms. Hasan read correctly the version in the English language. However, it does not correspond to the version in the Serbian language as between the words "killed", or rather I'm sorry, "Arrested" and the word "killed" there is no conjunction "and".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask the witness to read the last sentence of the first paragraph into the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can do that. The gentleman is right and I wanted to note that while reading but it's better that he did it. It says, "Arrested, killed, around 1.000 or up to 1.500 enemy civilians and soldiers." So there is no conjunction "and".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you read the -- this sentence literally? Can you please do it again, just read the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. "Arrested, were killed, around 1.000 to 1.500 enemy civilians and soldiers."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Hasan, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. Simanic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you carry on, Mr. Gajic has another comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just to correct the transcript, between the word "arrested" "were" and "killed" there were no commas in the original text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the original text, I don't see any comma. Thank you. Ms. Hasan, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember your exact words when you were first shown this document by the OTP in an interview in 2006?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I just glanced at this at the time, and that I said, "Oh, my God."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: This information that is in this first paragraph of the report, where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, when I said that as a battalion we did not have a zone of responsibility, the battalion also does not have trained personnel who would do that. So mostly the infantry battalions and bigger formations have intelligence men who are in charge of such things. We did not have this, and the information was received from our soldiers who were returning from rest, because we did not have any official information from the higher commands.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The way you received this information, was it the same way you received the information about the wounded soldiers that we've previously discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the wounded soldiers were something that could be seen and something that happened in Konjevic Polje itself. And this was something that happened somewhere. It doesn't say here where it happened. It's the general area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Since you didn't -- as I understand you to have just testified that you didn't have any intelligence of your own in the battalion, did you rely on your soldiers for information from -- coming from the field, from the region?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the region but, rather, our own soldiers who were returning from the places where they were taking rest. They would come back to Konjevic Polje and tell us what was happening, and this was probably included in order to turn attention of this unit to the fact that it could have problems. The higher command was supposed to check that and if it decided to react or do something about it, then it would order that unit or some other unit, which would step up the security in Konjevic Polje. But we never received such an order or such a piece of information. So we had to shift for ourselves, and I must note that at that moment, in Konjevic Polje, we did not have many troops available. There were only about 20 men or so. The weapons were really not good. These were old M-48 rifles and semi-automatic rifles, hardly a few automatic rifles. So that with that number of men and with such weapons, we fared pretty well and it's good that we didn't sustain greater losses.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The killing of enemy soldiers and civilians as referred to in this paragraph, would you have considered that to be a crime?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, for me, the biggest crime is when someone kills somebody who is tied. I don't know where, when and in what manner this happened. So I really cannot pass any personal judgement about that, whether it happened in combat or I don't know in what other way. When a war is being waged, you always have both the dead and the wounded on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If these people were first arrested and then killed, would that, in your view, have been a crime?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not a lawyer. I cannot say something like that. But for me personally, that really would be a crime. But it's not on me to establish anything and to judge anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have an objection because the witness is being asked to give a legal qualification and he explained earlier that in the report where it says, "Arrested killed," does not specify whether they were arrested or killed and whether his troops just heard it from soldiers who were passing by. He said that he didn't see it and he didn't have at his disposal a service which could check that and collect the relevant information, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, we received this answer and another answer to the last question. Please carry on, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The report then continues, and it outlines the tasks of the battalion. Under paragraph 2(a), we see a reference to the 1st Pioneer's company and it talks about building obstacles and fortifications in the area of the Vis facility and clearing mines in the region of Derventa. This, as well as -- sorry, as well as the fact that a squad was sent to clear mines in the Zeleni Jadar/Skelani region which had come back at that point. Is this what we were discussing before, when you were outlining to me what the Pioneer Company was doing on the 11th, 12th and 13th of July? Does that accord with what you told me?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you just read it. It means that this unit was never engaged to carry out one specific task, as a whole. Usually it had to carry out more tasks than it could. So when this unit came back from Skelani, the place is called Pribicevac, where they worked on de-mining, it came back and then it continued de-mining in Derventa. It says here "Sastavi," but it should say "Sastavci." It's a road leading from Derventa in the direction of Srebrenica. And some of them were working on the Vis facility. That's Osmaci, on Kalesija, it's quite far away, and another part maybe one or two soldiers, I'm not sure how many, remained in the barracks, were engaged on security tasks. I must say that as for Konjevic Polje, as a sector in geographical terms, one couldn't say where Konjevic Polje ends and Pobudje Brdo begins. One doesn't know where the border between municipalities are. I didn't know that at the time, nor was that important for us. But on Pobudje hill, where there was a power line leading towards Bratunac, there was a minefield, so that here the overlapping of these geographical notions cannot be taken literally because Pobudje as a hill belongs once again to the general sector, and therefore the border line is not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Is the information contained in this paragraph, then, accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it should be correct because it was written by a man who collected all this. It was the desk officer. He would collect all that and then type up the reports and he rarely made any mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's move on to subparagraph (b) which is on second page of the English version. It talks about the activities of the road and bridge company, that they were working for the Vlasenica PTT on a relay at Pogled, that they were constructing defensive positions in the area of the Vis facility and organising ambushes and engaging in combat activities with the enemy. Again, here would you say that the information in this subparagraph would -- was -- is accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps this could be a slip of the pen of the person who did this. I don't think that the road and bridge company could obstruct roads but it did do the works in the area of Vis. When something is obstructed it's usually the minefields that they mean here, and this was what the company was doing, and it was definitely located in the area of Vis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Then let's move to subparagraph (c), the engineering company or what you've referred to as the construction company, it states that they were carrying out construction work as ordered by the Drina Corps command in Crna Rijeka, at the Bisina barracks and at the Zaklopaca Limekiln does that accurately reflect the activities of the engineering company at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should reflect, perhaps, I don't know, because I cannot see it anywhere here, we also had a workshop in Vlasenica, which was part of the engineering company but it was a separate entity in Vlasenica, and it was in charge of minor repairs of buildings. It had a joiner and a painter and an electrician. So there were several repairmen, seven or eight of them, there. They were separated, and I see that they are not mentioned anywhere here among the work tasks but they were in another location. I'm not sure what the right military word for that is. They were attached to the Drina Corps command and they would reach agreements about works and tasks directly with them. Perhaps this is the reason why they are not included in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now if we can move to page 3 of the English version, under subparagraph 5, that would be page 2 of the B/C/S version, there is a reference here to an extraordinary event and it talks about two conscripts who were injured on the 13th of July 1995 at 0800 hours. Are these the same soldiers we were discussing earlier today?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the very same soldiers, Trifko Bandjur, Spaso Bandjur and Vasilije Orasanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now under subparagraph 6, under the heading "logistics," it reads: "Preparatory activities need to be carried out for the loading machine which will be engaged to bury the killed enemy soldiers. 50 litres of oil to be assigned for the task." Do you see that written there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, you have the original version in front of you. Do you see that there is a circle around "50 litres"?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we can now turn to the -- to subparagraph 9, if you look at subparagraph 9, which is -- yes, on the last page of the English version, it states under requests, "assign 50 litres of oil for the above task," and there is a handwritten note there that says, "Done." Would that have been -- would that handwritten note and the circle around the "50 litres" written with blue ink on the previous page of the English version have been a notation that you completed?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't us who entered the note. We just typed it out. And I don't know who wrote this note.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that your unit was involved in the burial of killed enemy soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Would your battalion make equipment available for projects that were not completed by your battalion but by others, if so ordered by the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the unit did everything only by order of the Drina Corps, and whatever the Drina Corps ordered to a subordinated unit, a battalion, it would issue an order and the order would specify in what manner the task would be carried out, whether we, if we had at our disposal such machines, would give such a machine, together with the operator, to somebody else, or we would be in charge of the task and then other machines would be attached to our unit. We did not have such cases when machines were attached to our unit but there were cases when we had to give our machines to others when roads were being built, if we had a machine at our disposal we would give it to another unit and it would be engaged for the need of this unit or for civilian needs. But then, in such a case, all the logistics and everything else, the manner in which this would be done and the tempo and so on, this would be given to the machine operator by the respective unit. I would also add that when it says under item 6, "logistics security," that it's necessary to carry out certain works for the work of a loader which will be engaged on burying. The loader is not a machine for digging. It just loads earth and other materials. There are other machines which are used for digging and which are specifically made in order to perform that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we please turn back to item 6 of the English version? Thank you. Ms. Hasan, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, there were massive graves that were being dug out in the vicinity of where your battalion was, and you've testified here that you had construction equipment in your battalion, including a loader. Are you telling us today that your equipment was not used in these massive operations that were going on?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, no. During the time that I spent there, I never issued such an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we turn to subparagraph 8, this is on page -- we've got the page already displayed. Under conclusions, forecasts and decisions, it states: "Continue organising ambushes to fight the enemy, infiltrated in the Pobudje hill, shift the focus of the fight against them there, destroy the enemy and liberate Pobudje hill as soon as possible. Continue with the 5th engineering tacks, increase security and vigilance measures in the region of Konjevic Polje." Would you say that this assessment or conclusion accurately reflects the measures that had to be taken at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must note once again, Pobudje Brdo, Pobudje hill, Konjevic Polje, these are the geographic names which are used all the time. Fighting against enemy with 20 men outside of a barracks, in order to do that you would have to have Special Forces rather than the old men that we had at our disposal. We tried to secure Konjevic Polje as a barracks as best as we could, but even without an order and let alone with an order issued to that effect, the barracks had to be secured, all of it. And as for the minefield, it began to the right of Konjevic Polje in the direction of Bratunac. So on the right-hand side, between the brook and the road, that was where the farthest guard post was. So we were supposed to close it off and not to let anyone pass through the minefield. It was a problem at night because we could not even change the guard. It was a greater problem at night. And it was rather a problem to secure all this. And the man who drew up this document wanted to illustrate the way that we had to work in the field or rather in Konjevic Polje, and once again, it's clear that we had to be engaged more in the field when it says, "Continue the work in which units of the 5th Engineering Battalion are charged with," it means that we were continuing to do one and the same thing, because when the superior command did not order us to bring back our men from the construction site, that meant that we normally just had to continue working as we had been doing up until that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. It's 10.30 and perhaps a good time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you indicate how much time you will need after the break to continue and finish your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I won't need -- I will probably need about 15 minutes to complete my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just noted a small mistake, on page 1 in line 21, it says, "Rule 74 bis" and it should say "Rule 94 bis."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It was a long time ago at that parts of the transcript. Before we break, I just would like to put one question to the witness. If we take it that you signed this document, did you sign it after having read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How should I tell you? I rarely read those documents. Actually I didn't read them. Because what was important or at least what I was told that was important is that we should simply write it out, everything where the G unit was engaged so that we could perform the duties that we can bearing in mind the number of men we had. And after each task we had to draft a report and that was the most difficult part to do. The most important thing to write out was how much fuel we spent because that was the most critical element in the whole setup. Excuse me, so I'm not an active officer. I'm a reserve officer. So there are some of my signatures that I indeed I did write down, although actually if you ask me I think it wasn't up to me to sign it as a deputy, because if the commander wasn't present, we would not do the handover. I don't know why he left and there was no handover which means that actually he was still a commander, not me. So this document should have been signed by a commander and then my signature should have been there as signing for the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We must have our first break now and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So as you can see, the Chamber is now complete again. Ms. Hasan, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we just have 65 ter 1910 displayed on the screen again?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, the fuel that we've been discussing, referenced in subparagraph 6, as well as paragraph 9, does that fuel relate to the mentioning in paragraph 1 of the people that were killed?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It does not relate to that. Since it is the logistics people who were requesting it, and this is the logistic department, they are simply requesting it from the higher command. I think that this was drafted by a professional man who heard that there were some killed people and decided to request it. If we receive such a request, then the use of this fuel can only be in accordance with a special order. As far as I know, we did not receive such an order and also we did not receive this fuel. It's a small quantity and nobody brought it over to us, as far as I know. So this wasn't actually used. And this thing that it says here, that it has been resolved, it means that somebody else wrote it. Only they know why it was done and how it was done. We didn't do it, and as far as I know, I'm not sure whether it was actually used.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, in relation to the first paragraph, which refers to the people being killed, why did you, when you first were shown this document by the Office of the Prosecutor, say, "Oh, my God"?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at first, I didn't read the whole of the report. In the first moment I thought that it was this unit who did it. And to me, it was a crazy thought that 20 soldiers, old and weak, could do something like this, while we only performed the tasks related to the security of the barracks. That's why I reacted like this. Because I have to emphasise it once again, I'm a reserve officer, and I simply took this as a template. Actually, I didn't write it myself. This is how these things were done all the time. And the administrative person drafted it in this particular way simply because I think that somebody had started it earlier on, probably the commander, and then the reports were drafted in this way. If you ask me, it's illogical that the 5th Engineering Battalion would have to contain anything related to the police company, because we didn't know anything about it. I don't know why it found its place in this report. Except maybe in order to inform the higher command that the police company is here in case they didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, you've mentioned a few times now that you were a reserve officer but can you tell us what your position was at the time this report was sent to the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the time, I performed the function of the deputy commander of the Engineering Battalion. I said that at the beginning. We divided the tasks between us and we used the same system of work all the time. So I did all the construction works, while other works related to administration and the military part of business so to speak, that's how I used to call it, I didn't do because I didn't know how to do these things. So it was the commander who did these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: This document that we are looking at, as the deputy commander, were you responsible for the information contained in that report that went to the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the engagement of this unit and the rules of engagement of this unit, I suppose I should be, but take a look at this. How could I be responsible for this police company that is also mentioned in here? There was no connection between the military and the police at this level. It never existed. I also said it already, I think, I don't know if you can probably find it in some transcript, but there was even some antagonism between the military and the police because the police used to be better supplied than the military, and also had at its disposal a far better logistics. So this antagonism actually grew by day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not quite sure I understand your answer to my question which was not whether you're responsible for the police but whether you were responsible, having signed this document, for the information contained in the report.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer. That's the essence of the problem. Am I responsible for information here? Well, take a look. Here, we find the police company mentioned, about which I know nothing. It was the administrative person who drafted it, who took care of all these things, and I simply signed it in hurry or sometimes even I signed blank papers so that they could go out as quickly as possible. This report wasn't really that important. We had separate reports for each construction site and that was important. When you drafted a report about the construction site, that was something very important, and then you really had to stand behind every single litre of the fuel reported, every single man-hour reported, and for that we had very accurate logs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, you testified here that you were -- you arrived in Konjevic Polje after the two soldiers of your battalion were wounded. Can you tell me when did you hear about these 1.000 to 1.500 men as mentioned in paragraph 1 of this document having been killed?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I learned about it. That's what happened that day, I suppose. Because the 14th of July means that it happened the day before it, because I suppose that when you write a report on the 14th of July then you actually report about what happened on the 13th of July. So it was simply rumours among our soldiers, and that's why it found its place here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you believe, sir, that 1.000 to 1.500 people were killed, as stated in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't either believe or disbelieve this. We don't have an organ which could determine that. This was more of an information to a superior command telling them that we learned that. And they can then go on and undertake certain measures in order to verify this information because we didn't have an intelligence organ or any other person who would be qualified to check this information because if we knew then we would probably say where they were and what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to tender this document as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P1769. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please -- I would like to have it on the screen because I would like to put an additional question related to this report to the witness. Ms. Hasan, have you finished this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have and I was going to offer the original to Your Honours if you would like to take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please. And I would like to ask the witness, this document is from the 14th of July. Where have you been that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember where I was that day. I said that after the wounding, I arrived, and that I found out only when I arrived that there were wounded. As far as my movements are concerned, I moved to all construction sites. You can see it here in the report, it says that the works are continuing on all the construction sites, and I had to go and ensure that the works went on, and those construction sites were quite far apart from each other. I had one in Bisina barracks, in the Sekovici municipality, then one above Vlasenica, then there was another construction site below Vlasenica, what's its name, Krecana and then there was another construction site that was in the preparation phase in Vlasenica so I had lots of work to do, and it wasn't my job simply to sit in Konjevic Polje. I had my tasks that I had to perform. That is why I can't tell you with any precision now where I was in each moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have you been in Konjevic Polje that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the 14th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you recall having been in the administration of your battalion, where those people who are responsible for the administration are located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's where we used to sit. We used a smaller house that had been destroyed earlier and then we converted it into small offices, and that's where we performed part of our tasks, when we were in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have you been in this location that day, 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to tell you again that I really cannot remember for this date. It was a long time ago and I cannot remember all the dates and where I was on those dates. If I was there on the 13th, late in the evening, I probably wouldn't go back in the night. Maybe I would then go again to visit the construction sites in the morning on the 14th because that was the kind of programme I usually had so it is possible that I was there for a part of the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My commander was Milenko Avramovic, the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where was he that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was not in the unit. I already said that. He was on leave, I think, that his wife and his child visited him and I think that he was somewhere in Serbia with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means you were really in charge as the acting commander of your unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in a sense, conditionally speaking, yes, because wherever I was at the construction site, I was also in charge of that construction site. You know, when my commander left, we didn't do any formal handover of duties. He continued to be the commander and I continued to be the deputy, and we continued performing our tasks in accordance with our agreement, meaning that I would do the construction part of the business and he would take care of the military part, and administrative part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You told us that it happened that you signed blank pieces of paper. Do you recall how frequently you did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I couldn't do it often. There were just a few combat reports. When I had to leave earlier, and then I would simply sign a blank paper in order not to leave the combat report undrafted. You know, all these reports basically repeat its contents, and I was told that the most important part was the part about the use of the unit, meaning what the battalion was doing, but the rest simply contains information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How did you know in these cases when you signed blank pieces of paper where to put your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since the administrative person was a professional, he had an idea about how much text there was going to be approximately, and then he fitted it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was this administrative person you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's written here, MB/MB. It was a staff sergeant who used to do all these things for us. He was old. He was either already retired or just about to retire. His name was Mirko but I don't know his last name. We used to call him Zajo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was he in a position to determine how many litres of oil you will need for carrying out this task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is the logistics. He simply picked up those data. He would simply collect all the data from everybody and then he would formulate it into the sentences and the text later on. And then he would draft a report like this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Tell me: Is it permitted for a deputy commander to sign a report without knowing the text of the report? That means a blank piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you: You know, we would usually agree the contents, what he was going to write. We would agree on that beforehand. And this is not the kind of document -- or at least I was told so, the kind of document that would be important, because it wasn't a combat unit. This unit did not take part in carrying out the tasks. So we didn't really have to spell out each task. The only important thing was to say where the unit was and where the unit was used so that we wouldn't get a task that we would not be able to carry out due to insufficient manpower. So in most cases, these combat reports were rather stereotypic and simply repeated their contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You just told me, in line 14 through 16, "You know, we would usually agree the contents, what he was going to write. We would agree on that beforehand." Was it the case with this report as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "agree," what I mean is each of us who had to take part in this would write a certain part. For instance if there were some changes in the kind of the use of this unit. And then you would write what had to be changed in relation to the previous report. I also didn't know where all the units exactly were and where they were engaged. So the guy in charge of the logistics would write his own part, he would collect all these other data, and then he would draft it into the shape of a combat report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to understand your -- the sentence, "each of us would who had to take part in this would write a certain part." Did you write a certain part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's why I'll telling you all this. If you take, for instance, the use of the unit, if there were some changes or a part of the unit would arrive to Konjevic Polje, then I would only write down this particular part. For instance, the 1st Pioneer company arrived from carrying out a task. Or if I had issued an order or assigned a task, then I would write it down, and if there are no changes, then he would incorporate this and simply copy the parts that hadn't been changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand your position. Can you nevertheless tell me which part of this report was written or drafted by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you, take for instance item number 2(A). Most probably it was I who said that this unit returned from de-mining of Zeleni Jadar. Most probably it was I who said that. He may have known it but I wrote it down because I knew it. If a unit goes to perform a certain task, it is done in accordance with an order because they have to act in accordance with that order. And then also this administrative person knows that such an order has been issued and he knows who went there and to carry out what task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And who was it who wrote the paragraph item number 1, "The enemy"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. It must be the staff sergeant who wrote this, most probably, based on what he heard, because all of us heard this in Konjevic Polje, you know, people were talking about it. People were talking about certain problems, that there were some killed people, some captured people, and most probably he wrote it in in order to draw attention to this because there were very few of us in the barracks. So we were not secure and things were going around, around us, and we didn't know which things exactly were going around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you saying that you were reporting rumours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we had no other way to do things because our unit did not have an intelligence organ who could go out and establish this or double-check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How could the Drina Corps command rely on your report signed by you, probably signed by you, in this combat report if there are only rumours? It's an official, regular, combat report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are rumours. I told you that if there was a need to double-check this, then the corps would go and double-check it, or if they thought there was a need to double-check it and if they knew that that was a fact then they wouldn't double-check it and then they would have to act in accordance with their own conclusion to see whether we are safe or not. If we were safe, the 20 of us, then they probably wouldn't even write to us, and in case we why not safe and secure then they would issue us some other order, if that was necessary in their view. They could maybe even call some other forces who would then come and help us to secure the barracks in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you come across an instance where somebody in your unit or somebody else signed instead of you, using your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you, I didn't really check these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It seems to be quite important, that this is your signature or the signature of another person. Did you authorise another person to use your signature at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never authorised anybody. I told you my signature is never the same. Every time it turns out slightly different. I never thought that this signature was really something important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, I would like to give back the original version of the report. Please carry on, Ms. Hasan. Judge Mindua has a question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. I don't know, you might have already answered this question. In the first paragraph, referring to the enemy, I see that it says that about a thousand to 1500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested and killed. Do you recall whether your battalion unit had arrested and then killed civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, at no point did I say that our battalion made the arrests. Those 20 or so soldiers could not have done that. Our battalion only provided security for the barracks in Konjevic Polje, and that is the only task that we could have comfortably carried out in view of our numbers and the weapons that we had at our disposal. When I speak about our numbers, I also want to mention the age of the soldiers who were there. And again, it doesn't state there, "arrested and killed." What is meant there is that they were taken out of operation, but it's not known how many of them were killed or wounded or captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So you had about 20 men with you. But you haven't answered my question. Was it usual to arrest people and then to kill them? Have you ever seen such things, so people being arrested and then, afterwards, being executed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see that. And I think that this is not something usual. This should not be a usual thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. The Presiding Judge has already asked the question that I wanted to ask, meaning why did you sign this paper, but you've already answered this question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan. Sorry, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just need to understand your testimony regarding to the compilation of a regular combat report as the one on the screen. Is it your evidence that more than one person contributed to the contents of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I said before, and according to what was required, it had to be a number of people. I can also say something that I forgot to mention before, and that is that this report is drafted in the Ekavica dialect, and I, you may have been able to notice, speak in the Ijekavica dialect. This automatically means that a number of persons participated in the drafting of this report. I'm not a professional in those tasks. Perhaps I would have drafted a different report which would not correspond to what was required. And that's why there was a person there who was entrusted with doing that job, with drafting the report -- reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. So you have different people writing the reports, inputting in this final report. How exactly did you input? Did you sit down, type your own portion, or did you write your report and give it to the person who finally finalised the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, nobody really wrote it properly. These would be just done along the general lines, adding only changes for a certain day, perhaps somebody requests -- would request that a certain change would be made in a particular part so this would be done very quickly and then the person would draft the report. At least, the way I understood it, the report doesn't have any weight because after that, it is used by the corps or by a larger unit, to understand what is going on in the field, in a particular unit, what the situation is, and what they would need to do. For example, to improve security or if people are not fully engaged to engage them on some other task and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Finally, we have a document on the screen, which is a combat report, in which you had an input as an individual. Did you actually type this portion on the report or somebody else typed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I mentioned it before who drafted it and who typed it, usually at the end of the combat report you would have initials. Here it's MB/MB, so that would be the answer to your question, that would be the person who drafted the report. That person did everything. If it hadn't been for him, we wouldn't even have half these documents done in this particular way. Perhaps we would have done them, yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now I have a follow-up question, sir. You said, answering a question by Judge Nyambe, "Perhaps somebody requests -- would request that a certain change be made in a particular part." How can I understand this answer? What does it mean? Somebody requests, particular -- to make a change in a particular part of the report? A change -- was there first a first draft and then a second draft after having made a change or was it a regular report sent every day and just with some additional remarks or what are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what you mean, change the report. I didn't mean for anybody to change the report. What I meant was, for example, if there were changes then, for example, just briefly I would say the unit returned from de-mining, so then he would know which unit and then he would put that in, if that happened when I was there. If I wasn't there, he would gather all the information himself and write -- write it in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to put to you what you said to one of the last questions. Page 43, lines 17 and the following. "Well, nobody really wrote it properly. These would be just done along the general lines, adding only changes for a certain day, perhaps somebody requests -- would request that a certain change would be made in a particular part." What does that mean? I'm referring to your own words about changes. What kind of changes are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Additions, something -- for example, I mentioned the 1st Pioneer company, the new thing would be that a part of that unit, I don't know how many men, came back from de-mining. So that would be a change in reference to a previous situation. So if I wrote that, I would write that just briefly, in case the person who was writing the report didn't know, then they would put that into the report. This is what I meant. Something new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You just said, "So that would be a change in reference to a previous situation." Do you mean a previous situation or a previous report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's not stated in the previous report, it would need to be put in the current report. Then we write down what happened. If I knew that such and such a unit returned, actually that group of people who went to Zeleni Jadar and Skelani for de-mining, I would just write, "The group returned from assignment in Pribicevac." And then he would just enter that, if it wasn't entered before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This doesn't help me to clarify the situation, especially in relation to the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this: Something that is new -- something new that happened, so if something new happened then that would be written in. I don't know if that would be entered into the previous day's report.
