I would write that just put it in general lines, write it by hand, saying a part of the unit came back from demining in Zeleni Jadar/Skelani and that was sufficient for him to check to see if he had entered that particular thing in the report from the previous day, whether that was something that he had already reported, and if not, then he would enter that regarding the engagement of the 1st Pioneer company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the other colleagues of your unit who contributed to this report, did they do that in the same way as you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably, if he wasn't there he -- if he was there, he would write it in, if he wasn't there he would give it to someone else saying, "Put that in, put that in," and that person would put that in and then do it, because who would know -- who else would know what was required by the logistics unit, what was lacking, what needed to be replenished, so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was it, I ask this question again, who gave the information which was put into paragraph 1, item 1, the enemy? There is a reference to the units of the 5th Engineering Battalion and the MUP. Who was it who gave this information so that the man who is just sitting in the office would be able to write that down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This information is something that we heard from soldiers who were returning to Konjevic Polje from their rest period. They conveyed this information to us. And that man entered it most probably in order to draw attention to events that were taking place around us. We didn't know anything about that, whether we were in danger or not and to what degree we were in danger. That was supposed to indicate that the superior command would need to check and issue a -- an adequate order if necessary, order to us, how to behave. It was our duty, as soon as we came to Konjevic Polje, to provide security for those barracks. I don't know whether that would be something that would be done with six soldiers or four soldiers at the guard posts, depending on the number of men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you and some others of your unit, you learned about this -- these 1.000 to 1.500 enemy people from your soldiers returning from the field; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the rest period. They would go home to rest for two or three days, then they would come back, they would report to Konjevic Polje, and then proceed to executing the same assignment or would be transferred to a different assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was not my question. I wanted to know, if I understood you correctly, that you learned about these 1.000 to 1.500 people from the soldiers coming back; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. I would like to put a question to you. You see that this document has triggered many questions and, of course, the Chamber has to find out about this document, and as far as I'm concerned, it's the first paragraph, where it is stated that between 1.000 and 1.500 civilians and soldiers were arrested and killed. And the Chamber has to find out what has happened. So I've listened to what you said very carefully. You said that there was a person who was drafting the report, and I understand that this person had to draft the main parts of that report. Even in this Tribunal, when the Registrar submits a report to New York, many people contribute to the drafting of the report, many sections contribute to the report. But the person, the final person, who signs the document has to checkup and has to find out whether he's not giving wrong information to his superiors, so you are an educated man, sir. What does a signature mean for you? You may sign any document and then you can send them to your superiors and you never check what's in it? Because this is not a propaganda document which was sending to the radio or the television, you were informing your superiors in order for them to give follow-up orders. So I would like to ask you for a last time a question: Did you check up the information about the thousand to 1500 people, we are talking about civilians and soldiers, who were arrested and killed? So this would be the last time that I would ask you this question, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I replied and told you what I know, and that is that -- how we found out about it and what we found out. The unit where I was did not have any trained people who would be able to check this because this is something that is done, checked by the intelligence organ. We didn't have such an organ in the unit, and we had to somehow protect ourselves or, in a way, inform the superior command that we had heard that something was happening and that we didn't know what it was and that, of course, we were concerned about how things would develop. This is why this was put in, so that the superior command could check it because they also knew that we didn't have an intelligence organ who would be able to provide relevant data there that would be accurate. This is generally what we heard and what we reported to the superior command, and it was up to the superior command to react if there was a problem relating to the security of the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough. So the report was not properly drafted. You might have used the verb "may" or "might" about a thousand to 1500 people might have been arrested and killed. Or for the first sentence, you could have said, "A large -- it is possible that a large enemy group was infiltrated," and then you could have added that you hadn't double-checked the information because for me, I still -- I still have a doubt, I'm still sceptical about the number of people who had been arrested and killed as stated in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned that it was some 20 people. It's impossible that they would be able to do something like that, to provide security for the barracks and to do this. This is why this was put into the report so that the superior command would have to do something if they assessed that we were under threat because there were only a few of us. We were not properly armed, and elderly people could not really fight seriously in any type of enemy attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in other words, you wanted to disinform the superior command in order for them to react and you were expecting a positive reaction from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was not able to establish whether this was erroneous information from the soldiers or not who were returning. I already mentioned that we didn't have an intelligence organ and this is why. Had I had an intelligence organ in the unit, then this would have been processed by the intelligence organ and they would have said, "Well, this is erroneous information. Please do not write that in the report." This is at least what I think and what I know about the way official correspondence is carried out in the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, sorry for this lengthy interruption. You should proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the place? The settlement of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know it. It's a settlement between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: How many kilometres away from Konjevic Polje is Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely. I think it's about halfway between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, you work in that area. Approximately how many kilometres is it from Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said halfway, then it's about 12, 13, 14 kilometres. That would be that, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And have you seen the famous video that's been -- that was broadcast all over the world of dead bodies piled up in front of the Kravica warehouse? Have you seen that video?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I didn't see that video footage, but I heard on television that they talked about it and about what was done there in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Were you aware that 1.000 plus bodies were exhumed from a mass grave in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear that after, once this exhumation was completed. Until then I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And how many kilometres is Konjevic Polje from Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Glogova, the place, is near Bratunac, as far as I know. It's very near Bratunac. It's some three to four kilometres from Bratunac, which means that it's some 20 kilometres away from Konjevic Polje, Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, you may commence your cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Peace in this house, peace to all present. I would like today's day and the entire trial ends in accordance to God's will and not as I wish. I welcome the witness, I would like to wish him a pleasant stay here amongst us and also a pleasant and fortunate return home. I thank him for coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since we are speaking the same language I would like to ask you after I put the question to you and say thank you, I would like you to pause for some five seconds with your answer until the interpreter has translated and then you will be able to see actually the pace by watching the screen, which will show the progress of the translation. So you wait until the typing on the screen stops before you begin answering. After the examination-in-chief, today I -- the Prosecutor, Ms. Hasan, for you to be able to follow more easily I'm going to start from the more recent questions that were put to you. On page 50 of this transcript, today, Judge Mindua - actually on page 48, line 1, Judge Mindua asked you about the number of prisoners your administrator entered as a piece of intelligence data into the collective daily report that was submitted to the corps command. You were also asked whether you checked this information. On the basis of that, my question is: Data about the enemy that is submitted to the superior command on the basis of your information, was that something that was checked by you or was that sent to the commands to be checked? If you don't have an intelligence organ, who is supposed to actually check the information that is being submitted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are much more knowledgeable in this area than I am, and that is why you're putting this question. I'm trying to explain this the whole time because we, in the unit, did not have a single organ that would be capable of checking this information. I, as a layman, if I can call myself that, in relation to military administration, was told that this would be something that the superior command would check and that they will give us information about how to proceed further. This is something that this warrant officer knew for sure, he was also a professional, so this is the way he did this particular thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us if anyone of your acquaintances from the unit, from your lower-ranking units or superior unit, was accountable for providing inaccurate information about the enemy in each item of the report? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that anyone was held accountable for inaccurate information that was submitted on the enemy situation. I was not held accountable, nor was I ever called out by anyone for providing this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether the information about the enemy, which is the first item of every report, are submitted on the basis of the information collected up to that point, and if they are not checked, can anyone be held responsible for that by the superior command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that anyone was held responsible. I tell you that again. But we didn't have any way to check and this is why we would send them unchecked information and we waited for the response of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have soldiers from the entire zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps in the composition of your unit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. The soldiers were from all areas of the Drina Corps's zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have construction areas which you had to carry out works at in all areas of the zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In all places except in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your desk officer always state the information which he received from the field from the soldiers who would come back from the places where they were taking rest, whether it was at home or from the construction sites?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we only had information about the enemy in that area and at that time. We didn't have anything else. And the information was only based on what we were told by the soldiers who were coming back from rest or from leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, for the transcript, though, one can conclude from your answer, did your soldiers take rest in the barracks or did they go to their homes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All soldiers who were sent to take some rest were taking the rest at their homes. Depending on how long they had worked, that would determine the number of days that they were given for rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you remember, we heard a lot of information about what you just said but I would like to introduce some new information and something new that you learned. Can you answer my question, please? Did your desk officer always enter the new activities of the unit and the new information as compared to the previous one, or would he mention that the task that had been issued earlier would be stated once again? When you said that he did not enter any changes, the changes only had to do with actual changes of activity, not the changes in terms of the contents of the report. I'm not sure if you understood me and can you please answer this question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the works that we had to carry out would still be entered, but if there was a change, then it would be added. So let me explain. If, for example, we worked on a passive reflector and if one unit had to work about that, but the road and bridge unit also some work to do at Vis and in some other places, that would remain in a report but an addition would be added that the unit which completed its part of the task had returned to the barracks or had now moved to another construction site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber, and for the transcript, whether the managers of construction sites in various places within your zone of responsibility and platoon commanders of the engineer's company did make any contributions for the daily report to the desk officer who would collate all the information to produce the daily report for the whole brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes they would. If somebody wasn't there, myself or somebody else, they would directly give the information they had to the desk officer, for example that they returned or that they were going to a specific construction site in accordance with a specific order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware whether your desk officer sometimes called parts of the unit on the telephone, because they were dispersed across the whole zone, to ask them what they were doing and what was the new task in which they would be engaged and how much time they would need to complete the previous task?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it was possible, he sometimes did that, because he also had various tasks to perform. He wasn't just sitting there and typing up reports. But our communication line was very poor, and most of the time it wasn't working. I said that we had a field telephone where the cable was on the ground, and we generally had a problem communicating with the higher-ranking units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We have in front of us your report dated the 14th of July 1995. It's 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And can we please slow it on the screen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you asking for P1769? That's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, witness, if we would now have a look at this, this is the report dated the 14th of July 1995. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As for the two soldiers who are mentioned in the report, were they wounded on the 14th or on the 13th? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that the report was only written on the following day, on the 14th, that is to say one day after they were wounded? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't have been written in any different manner. It was written on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It doesn't say here when this report of yours was submitted to the corps command. But was it submitted by the 1500 hours on that day, the 14th? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when it was submitted, but sometimes the reports were late. We always had problems because of this, because they would just tell us a few words to upbraid us and it would end there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that the report could have been written on the basis of information that was available as early as on the 13th? I mean that the desk officer who drew up these reports had them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On several occasions, you said that sometimes you would sign blank documents that were to be turned into reports as the deputy commander or that sometimes you signed it without even glancing at it knowing that the warrant officer was a professional so I won't ask you anything more about that, but I will ask you the following: Do you know if you look at the last page of this report, and can we please show it on the screen, here it is, it says, down there, MB/MB. Do you know that the MB means that these are the initials of the person who drew up the document and the initials of the person who typed it up? On the left side, it's the person who signed it, and the right initials are the initials of the person who drew up the report. Do you know that this is the rule for official correspondence?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that. But I once accidentally asked about that and it was told to me that the persons of those who drew up the document and wrote it were placed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a look later on at the reports which were written by the corps commander and other officers so we'll see that it's always -- the initials of one person that are on the left and the other one on the right. The one who is writing should be on the left and one who is typing it up should be on the right so that one could know through whom secret and confidential military information could flow or leak. Thank you. As it says here, MB/MB, does it mean that one and the same person drew up and typed up this document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by what's here, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it mean that on the 14th of July 1995, this person, whose initials are MB/MB, typed up this daily report which was sent to the corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not ask you much about item 1 because both the Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber asked you about that and you answered as you have. I will ask you just one question. The first item, concerning the enemy, does it include all the information that the unit has about the enemy both in the field and in the zone?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how they explained to me, write everything you know, and then as you don't have an organ who will check that, then either the superior command will check it and send you feedback about the unit's further activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please see in e-court the following document? P1603, which was sent by the Drina Corps command to the Main Staff so that we could see whether your information was included in the amalgamated daily report which was sent out from the corps. Thank you. Thank you. We can see it now. This is the report to the Drina Corps command written on the 14th of July 1995. It is actually addressed to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and it is called the regular combat report. You can see item 1, concerning the enemy, which talks about the northwestern part of the front where I shall quote: "In the general Kalesija area, Pohunjak, Osredak and Kutici a large buildup of enemy forces was observed, their objective by attacking from the front is to link up with a group which had pulled out from the Srebrenica enclave." And the following sentence says, "In the morning, the enemy from the Gorazde enclave fired with infantry weapons on the Sjenokos and Crvljevac [phoen] village sectors but it did not affect our forces. It is quiet in the remaining part of the front in the corps's zone of responsibility." This is all that it says about enemy and it's the information dated the 14th of July 1995. My question is this: Do we see anywhere here the information about the enemy which you submitted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, I cannot see a single information that came from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. My command [as interpreted] is then this: Did the corps command then make a selection of what they would report about and what may be interesting for the Main Staff and what they will report to the Main Staff and also about the truth of the information that it could send?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they probably made their own assessment and selection of the information about the enemy that they would include here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Can you see in the first sentence here, that by observation, a large buildup of enemy forces was observed? And then they go on to discuss the aim of their attack. So do they talk about exact information and exact intentions of the enemy here or is this just the assessment?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, decidedly, this is the exact information and also the intention of the enemy, which is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now please show page 2 of this document in e-court? Thank you. Can you see under item 8, that it says, conclusions, forecasts and decisions for further action? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it a duty of each battalion and each unit, which submitted information to the corps, to make the conclusions, forecasts and decision for further action which was then collated by your desk officer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the information we had because we didn't receive any other information it was his duty to draw some conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On several occasions you were asked about the meaning of these conclusions, whether the conclusions were conclusions, forecasts and intentions or, as in this case, decisions of the corps command which is a higher command and which does make decisions. As for your specific report, was it also a possibility for the person who drew up the document to freely make some conclusions and assessments?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was free to do that because we did not receive any instructions or orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, thank you. During the examination-in-chief, the Prosecutor asked you the following, about item 8 in your report, which is entitled, "Conclusions, forecasts and decisions," and you were asked this: Whether someone could be held responsible and whether you are aware that anyone was held responsible, prosecuted or held responsible on the basis of chain of command for the conclusions and decisions if they were contrary to the main order for carrying out certain tasks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our conclusion was not made on the basis of the main order, but on the basis of our view, and if we made a mistake, then the superior command should suggest this to us in the appropriate manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you say clearly in the last sentence: "Continue with carrying out the works which the units of the 5th Engineers Battalion is carrying out and increase the measures of security and vigilance in Konjevic Polje sector"?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote that for this reason; if I hadn't received a new order that means that the previous orders were priority, and I had strict deadlines for completing works on specific facilities, and this is why I mentioned that in the conclusion, that we were continuing to carry out the works on the previous tasks we had been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If on the previous day two of your soldiers were wounded as the report says, is it then logical that, as you said here, the measures of vigilance and security in the Konjevic Polje sector where they had been wounded would be increased? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation was out of control. As soon as you have wounded men, then that's the factual situation, you have to take measures to protect other soldiers and workers in Konjevic Polje because it was no longer an assumption. Now we had two wounded men. We had a conflict that had broken out in the Konjevic Polje barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In item 8 of your report, in conclusions, forecasts and decisions, do you make these on the basis of actual elements of what happened and which could threaten the unit for the security of which you were responsible?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my view, that was the actual factual situation because if you had two wounded men, then you could have more. I didn't know what the intentions of the enemy were. He could attack the barracks. So you could -- you had to take all the possible measures that you had at your disposal to defend the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As the enemy also knew that the barracks was situated there, and that it's possible that they knew which mines and explosives were there, was there a danger that they might seize these mines and explosives in case the enemy took over the barracks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that, not only the ordnance within the warehouse, but they maybe could have de-mined the minefields and then used them for their own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go towards the enemy or did the enemy arrived in the zone of the barracks in Konjevic Polje on its own?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not go anywhere from Konjevic Polje. They came to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were your soldiers wounded while performing duty at the guard posts or were they wounded in some other sort of combat activity?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My soldiers were wounded at the guard post number 6, while performing the task of securing the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So item 5, written on the 14th of July at 0800 hours where it mentions the wounding of those two soldiers at guard post number 6, is it true?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already told you, I wasn't there but those who were there, they wrote exactly what happened that day at -- at the 0800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Take a look at the report that is currently on the screen in front of you. And can you take at the bottom of the page, where it said, "received," can you see when the encryption people in the Main Staff received it? Look at this. 14th of July 1945.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you can also see the signature. Does that mean that this report arrived to the Main Staff only at 1945 on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So does that point to the conclusion that every day a report would have to be filed with the Main Staff until 8.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's most probably true but I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. You don't know that. But can you tell us, would you allow for the possibility that your unit also received a certain deadline for filing its reports so that they could be then incorporated in a report going higher up?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now take a look at 1D571?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment, before we do that, I would like to put a question in relation to this document on the screen. Can we have back item 8 in both languages, please? In English, it's page 2, I think. I would like to receive a comment on this part, with the headline, "decision." The second sentence is the following. I quote: "Part of the forces in coordination with the MUP, Ministry of Interior, will check the territory behind the lines. Detect, block, arrest and disarm, disperse, Muslim forces" and so on. Next sentence, I quote: "Part of the forces will check and set up ambush operations with the MUP along the Muslim group's axis of withdrawal completely secure the" and there is mentioning a certain line. I see here a decision of a higher level above you about the coordination of the army and the MUP. We talked about a possible coordination of these units earlier today. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, are you referring to my report and not this report sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In your report, there was also a mentioning of cooperation with the MUP and you said you didn't know anything about that. Now we see here in this report also a decision about a common cooperation of these different units. And I would like to know what you know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you were listening carefully, and I think you did, you would have noticed that I emphasised that there was a permanent police check-point at the intersection in Konjevic Polje. They controlled part of the intersection and whatever else they controlled. Our first neighbour, looking from the guard post number 6, is this very check-point. In between there is a minefield. Not literally in between but slightly up there. So you could say that one of our guard posts controlled one end of the minefield so that nobody could enter into the barracks using the path between them and the minefield. They were our neighbours, you know we couldn't kick them out because they too were part of the forces securing this area of Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was not asking about the presence of these units but about the cooperation. Here it is said, "part of the forces in coordination with the MUP, will check" and so on. Was there a coordination or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we talk about coordinated action, we can only talk about it if we understand it that they have to observe one part of the minefield that was in Konjevic Polje. That was the only coordinated action. If they were defending that part then it was quite logical that they would also be taking part in securing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we should -- Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. I would like to go back to Exhibit P1603, which is the regular combat report issued on the 14th of July 1995 by Major-General Radislav Krstic. And in this report, the enemy is mentioned, and General Krstic does not talk about the 1.000 or 1.500 civilians or soldiers that were arrested and killed. Of course, this could be explained in such a way that having checked the information in the report, he felt that it was not accurate. But I note that in your report, which is Exhibit P1769, we have the same date, 14th of July 1995. So exactly the same date as that of Major-General Krstic's report. So I'm rather at a loss. I'm wondering why the Major-General's report does not mention the civilians that are mentioned in your report. Could that be, and this is a possibility, so I'm asking for your input here, could it be that your 14th of July report arrived in the evening while the Major-General's report was sent to his superiors beforehand, which means that the Major-General did not have time to include what was mentioned in your report? So my question is the following: I would like to know when the report reached the 2nd Corps. I'm talking about your 14th of July report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our reports, as I have explained, did not go regularly, but I think that they would always arrive during the day. They would always arrive to the corps during the day. And if not, then there would be problems with us. We would be singled out for criticism. I didn't see it written here, but I think that they should have read our report, and I think that they have formed their opinion on it, if they deemed it necessary, or if they thought that it was truthful. So if this report doesn't contain it, if, as you say, our report arrived too late, then it should be contained in the following report of theirs. Here, I don't see any such mention. Now I had a chance to read it in more detail. And he says that the main body of the forces from the Srebrenica enclave had already passed Konjevic Polje and reached Udrc so obviously he must have had some assumptions and information and he must have made some checks because Udrc is higher than Cerska in the direction of Tuzla. It's quite far away from Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need our second break now and then you should continue with the next document, Mr. Tolimir. We will resume five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said, if something was not entered into your report going towards the corps and into the report of the corps going upwards on the 14th, then you should be able to find it in the report written on the 15th. So let us take a look at the following. When was it that you sent the first information on the wounded to the corps? Can we take a look at P1768? Thank you. So here we can see that your unit informed the corps command on the 13th that Spaso Bandjur and Milan Orasanin were wounded. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know did the corps command receive this report?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they should have, it should have arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have now P1767? Thank you. Okay. Here we can see another report, sent by your battalion, and in the first sentence, we see the following. "Pursuant to your record strictly confidential 05/1-207 of 16th of June" and so on and so forth, "We are forwarding you the data on the wounded members of the 5th Engineering Battalion." So my question is as follows: Judge Mindua asked you why you sent two reports. Do we find here exactly what is the basis for sending reports?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we take a look at this, you can see it. I don't really know this order. I haven't seen it. But if you take a look at it, you will see that there was a change in the system of registering killed and wounded. I assume that, most probably, there is also another form that went as an attachment to this report, and then it was obviously sent pursuant to the order 05-1-207. And it was sent on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us take a look at what you said just before the break. If something wasn't included on the 14th, it should have been included on the 15th. Can we take a look at P1604? That's the report for the 15th. Report sent by the Drina Corps to the Main Staff. Thank you. So this is the report to the 15th of July. And we can see item 1, the enemy. The first paragraph contains the information of the -- about the Kalesija-Kladanj part of the front. The second paragraph talks about the front facing Gorazde. The third paragraph talks about the Zepa enclave and the last paragraph describes the activity of the enemy on the Tuzla-Zvornik and Orlovo-Kladanj axis. You can see the commander here announces an interim report. So can you see anywhere under item 1 the information provided by your analyst from your battalion? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any of the information that we had forwarded to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we find anything in this report that pertains to wounded or killed Muslim soldiers in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot find any such thing in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now take a look at page 2 of this report? Thank you. All right. We are waiting for the second page. Here at the bottom you can see that it was received on the 15th of July at 1945, just like the report of the previous day. It was also at 1945. In English it's the following page. Thank you. So we can see from this that the corps reports arrive to the Main Staff mostly until 2000 hours, which means that a lower units send their reports to the corps command earlier; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it must be like that, otherwise how would they report the final report -- how would they compile the final report?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here we can see again conclusions, projections and decisions for further action. So that was what the commander decided on the 15th that is to be done on the 16th. Can you find here at any place the zone where your barracks is located or are they simply talking about Udrc which is the territory further on towards Tuzla, further on from Konjevic Polje where the enemy had already evacuated by that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here you can only see the mention of Udrc and there is no mention of our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how far is Srebrenica from Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is about 35 kilometres between Srebrenica and Konjevic Polje, and then Udrc is - now let me calculate - about 15 kilometres from Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In order for us to gain a clear picture, especially for those who never visited that area, looking from Srebrenica, what is further away, Udrc or Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you add the two values, you get the distance between Srebrenica and Udrc which means that Udrc is about 50 kilometres from Srebrenica, meaning it's further away than Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've been asked whether you, in your report, under item 8, mention the cooperation with MUP. Can we have now on the screens your report so that we can see whether there is anything like that contained in it. That was your first report, P1 -- it's the report dated the 14th of July, sent by your battalion to the corps command, one second, I'll find it, it's 1769, yes. Thank you, Aleksandar. Thank you. Could we look at page 2, please, in e-court? Thank you. We can see at page 2, item 8, where it says, "Conclusions forecasts and decisions." Can you please read it for yourself and then I will put some questions to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: In paragraph 8, Conclusions, forecasts and decisions, did you make any kind of decision or conclusion regarding the cooperation of your unit with the MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't bring -- make any conclusions or issue any orders in relation to cooperation with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The person who wrote the report for your activities that day, did they state anything about your cooperation with the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing else written about cooperation with the MUP other than what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I was thinking of paragraph 8. I was imprecise, perhaps. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could the Trial Chamber please have document 0190 and P1604?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should stay for a moment with this document, please. I would like to see the next page in English. And now I would like to see the first paragraph again in both languages, the first paragraph. Could you please comment on the first paragraph, "A large enemy group was infiltrated in the region of Pobudje Brdo and the region of Konjevic Polje. Units of the 5th Engineering Battalion and the MUP successfully resisted the enemy." Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is primarily meant here is this: Since there were no losses, there were no deaths, and the enemy did not enter the barracks, so this was considered a success.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now you should continue with the document you wanted to see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to see 1D571 on the e-court, please. And while we are waiting I would like to say that this is an interim report by the corps command for the 14th of July, signed by General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We are looking at this report and it should include the data, this is a report General Krstic sent to the Main Staff, and the Drina Corps command. This is sent by General Krstic, interim combat report, the first paragraph contains data about the enemy, it says: "The enemy put up a strong resistance to our forces, particularly on the Podzeplje-Brloznik axis and so on. And it said it fired on Zepa and around Zepa and also it relates to Krstic's answer where he says, "I have decided after ordering the combat alignment at the achieved lines to forcefully extend the attack and capture Zepa as soon as possible." Could the second page of the document please be shown in e-court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that there is no English translation available at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Actually, we don't need to look at page 2. What we need to do is just to look at the bottom of this page to see when the document was sent to the Main Staff. We can see at the bottom that the document was sent on the 14th of July and that it was received at the Main Staff at 2312 hours, which means that up until the 14th at 2312 hours there are no other data on your unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, that is what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is an English translation of this document, and perhaps when discussing it we should display that one as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be very helpful. We have on the screen only two times the same B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It seems that the English version was not uploaded on to e-court, so it is available on Sanction, and Janet tells me that that can be displayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we should put both side by side, if that is possible. I was told it's not possible to see -- to look at both at the same time because it is not uploaded in e-court yet. The problem can be solved later. At the moment, it's not possible to put both on the screen. If necessary, we could try to print one version and put it on the ELMO and then we switch -- or we can switch from one to the other. I don't know how to deal with that. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You can look at the copy in English. I have the original in my hand. After that, because there is a translation, I would like to tender this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But first you should continue your questioning to this document or have you finished that already?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, I would like to put my last question to the witness regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this interim report contain any data relating to the activities or the zone in which your unit is located? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I read this, I didn't see anywhere that anything referred to the area where our unit was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this interim combat report by General Krstic of the 14th of July at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question to you is, on the basis of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please be patient for a moment. We will mark it for identification. It will be then very shortly received into evidence when we have the official translation uploaded into -- in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned exhibit number D156, marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, on the basis of the documents that we've seen of the 13th, 14th and 15th that was dispatched to the Main Staff, does any of those documents contain any information about your unit, its activities, or anything else other than the data about the wounding of two soldiers? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't read any data like that about my unit anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And your soldiers, were they wounded at the permanent guard post number 6 or were they away from the guard post when they were wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wounded while they were at the permanent guard post number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what does it mean, permanent guard post? Is that a location in the barracks in order to provide security for the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were transferred to Konjevic Polje, the commander issued an order to provide security for the barracks. It would be combined security for the barracks, consisting of minefields and guard posts. There were six permanent guard posts and if there were more soldiers, for example sometimes in the winter there were more of us, and in order to utilise all the soldiers present, then there would be two more temporary guard posts that would be included under that particular order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During the examination-in-chief, on page 4, line 10, you said, "We learned that a group of the B and H army was passing." On the basis of that, my question is: Did you learn about this only after they opened fire at your guards near your barracks, or did you get this information from soldiers who were coming from different areas back to your unit after resting?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found out about it from soldiers who were coming back. The wounding that occurred after that, confirmed that there was something there that could present a problem for our unit, in our barracks, and that is why this was followed by the conclusion that combat readiness measures should be increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You used the term "passing". Does somebody who is passing by wound soldiers at the guard post or were they actually trying to get through to the area under the control of the B and H army?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used the term "passing through" or "passing by" there because up until then we didn't have any problems. They were passing by next to us before. As for places where there were some combat actions and contact with our soldiers, that did happen, but when this happened, when our soldiers were wounded, that meant that this was a direct contact between the two sides and then this was followed by these two soldiers of ours being wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The activities of the enemy in relation to a stationary unit, when two soldiers are wounded, which constitutes 20 per cent of the overall number of soldiers who were in your barracks, does that constitute just passing by or does that constitute an attack on your barracks and your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We constituted -- we understood that to be a direct attack, as they were passing by our barracks. We didn't have enough men or weapons so we had to pay attention to that more than anything else, any kind of sabotage in terms of our depot could be devastating for all the people in that area. So then this was a problem, like I said -- I mentioned we also had two minefields that were about two kilometres in length, I don't know how broad they were. And if you didn't guard those minefields they were also exposed to de-mining and to being utilised on the part of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. [French on English channel]. In the area of combat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For a moment we had French translation on our channel but now it's correct again. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do combat rules provide for a unit in combat, which is deployed somewhere or which is at a permanent location and is secured by minefields, by a wire fence and other protection, depending on what other protection it has, is that provided for under the rules?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what the commander told us and he probably put that in writing as well, since he informed us about this, what he said was that all means are to be used to secure the barracks, and its surrounding area, amongst other things, since we didn't have enough personnel and we knew that we would be working on all of these construction sites, we knew that there would be a problem with forces and that is why the defences were strengthened by the minefields. We didn't have anything else available so this is why we laid down the minefields and we put up the permanent guard posts as well for the same purpose. Later he took all of us to show us the exact location of the minefield so that we wouldn't activate the mines ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber was this minefield laid down immediately after the unit deployed at Konjevic Polje or was this something that was laid down on the 13th? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done immediately when we came to Konjevic Polje. As soon as we created conditions for any kind of stay in Konjevic Polje, the commander ordered for the fortifications to be built in that area which was inaccessible because of the size and the lay of the area, so he decided, because it was inaccessible, to augment the guard posts with the minefields.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm sorry for being imprecise, can you please tell us what time that occurred, what time of the year, what date it was?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we came in 1994, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's clarify for the transcript, the minefields that you were questioned about here, were they laid down in 1994 and 1995 on the day of the attack by the Muslims who were trying to get past by you after leaving Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minefields were laid immediately, in 1994, in order to compensate for the low number of personnel there so that we could step up the security during our stay in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During the examination-in-chief you were asked about the locations that are closer to Konjevic Polje and so on. My question would be this: Did your soldiers who were in Konjevic Polje on the 13th, leave the barracks in Konjevic Polje? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not leave the barracks. They stayed there and the result of that was that the people who were standing guard at night had good relations with them because fear is stronger in the men during the night which is normal so they didn't leave their guard posts nor Konjevic Polje nor the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether your soldiers from the location where they were went into action in any way, did they fire at all, because you explained that they had old weapons.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not fire and that would include the two who were wounded. They had no time to react because they were wounded first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, as the Prosecutor asked you several times, why you said during some interview, "Oh, my God"? Was it a surprise for you when you saw the piece of information that made you exclaim, "Oh, my God"?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the order itself, I didn't read it in detail so at first I thought that it said that our unit had done that and I knew that it wasn't capable of something like that, particularly considering the number of men we had at our disposal at Konjevic Polje at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As the officer who was in charge of the unit at the time, do you think on the basis of your military expertise, that the person who entered the information about the enemy while typing up the report did not explain how he came to the information which he included in the report and then submitted to the corps command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now, when I read it, I think that perhaps he should have processed that in much more detail, but at the moment, we just thought that it should be mentioned probably, just mention it and then the superior command is the one to react or not to react, and then we would know what the situation in the territory that was around us was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Considering the general situation in the field at the time, did the members of your unit feel any concern about their safety during the night and during the day and so on and so forth considering the rumours that were going around and which you forwarded to the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could they not feel concerned? Once the rumours start going around, then things become inflated and once they reach the last person who hears this, the news becomes alarming. You have such problem in the army, when there is had hear say that was the situation. I was afraid someone might panic and leave Konjevic Polje which would really be a problem but no one left their posts including the guards which means that this had an effect on them because we never had the change of guard during the night. A certain number of men would stay in their posts as guards throughout the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for the answers you have provided during your testimony. Thank you for coming here. The Defence asked as many questions as it believed was necessary. I wish to thank you. I wish you a pleasant stay here and a pleasant return home, a happy return to your family.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have completed this part of my cross-examination in relation to this witness. I wish to thank you everyone who helped me and the witness and I wish to excuse myself before everyone because of the speed because I thought that I would have more questions to ask in the same time period. Thank you, Witness, I wish you a happy return home and God bless you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Hasan, do you ever re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'd like to start with Exhibit P94, page 37, please. These are the photo exhibits of Jean-Rene Ruez.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is the elementary school in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Was this where your battalion was based?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our battalion was not located at the primary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Where -- in which school was your battalion based, then?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not accommodated at a school at all. It was on the other side, at the back of the school, there was one classroom which we had turned into a dining room, but it had no contact with the main road. You couldn't enter it from the main road. It was at the back side where the boiler room was. That was another room there which was turned into a kitchen, and another room that we used as the dining room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: But, sir, are you talking about behind this building, this school?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The entrance was from the back side of the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And the -- sorry, is this where you had your offices?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I explained that. Behind the school, there are some smaller buildings too. They were ruined, and two or 300 metres behind the school, to the hill there, were the offices and then I'm not sure how many metres away was the warehouse, and then the logistics security, that was the logistics platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that a witness has testified, who said that they were housed in this shack that we see in this photograph, the left of this photograph, who was housed there in the evening of the 13th -- on the 13th of July and was subsequently sent for execution -- I'm sorry, my apologies, the morning of the 13th of July, and was subsequently sent for execution at the banks of the Jadar River? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first time I hear that, because we were not using these premises at all. The police were there, those who came and had shifts there and at the check-points. We were not using these premises at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, first, Mr. Tolimir wants to say something, and we are now at the end of today's hearing. How much time do you need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: There is a couple of documents I'd like to go through so it may take a good 15 to 20 minutes to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we have to continue with that tomorrow of course. Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I only had an objection because no references were given to the witness, and he's asked about something that others stated or others did. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to adjourn for today. Ms. Hasan, I would like to let you know the Chamber would appreciate if during the re-examination you always could indicate the relation to that specific part of the cross-examination. We have to adjourn but before we do that I have to tell the parties that there was a need for rescheduling our hearing on Wednesday because we had many problems with different Chambers to combine, especially in relation to those Chambers, two of the members of this Bench are involved in. We are sitting on Wednesday in the morning instead of the afternoon. This is the only change. And the other Chamber will sit in the afternoon. We adjourn and resume tomorrow in the afternoon in this courtroom, 2.15, and, sir, please be reminded that it's not allowed to have contact to either party during the break. The court usher will assist you in relation to the break. Thank you very much. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of February, 2011, at 2.15 p.m. 25
